title: Mahala 1, mahala 5
hookLine: every Guru signed as Nanak; the heading mahala with a number tells you which Guru
last: BANI — A WEAVER'S SONGS BESIDE A KING'S.

cards: Here's a puzzle. You reach the last line of a hymn in the Granth, and it says: Nanak says this. Easy, Guru Nanak wrote it.
The next hymn also ends with Nanak. And the next. But some of these hymns praise the pool of Guru Ram Das, a pool dug long after Guru Nanak was gone.
They speak of things he never lived to see. So who's writing, when every one of these poets signs with the same name?

teach.h: THE HEADING: A RAGA AND A NUMBER.
teach.b: Look at the top of a hymn, not the bottom. There's a heading: first the raga, then a word and a number. Sri Rag, mahala 1.
Gauri, mahala 3. Asa, mahala 5. Today's word is mahala, and the number tells you which Guru.
Mahala 1 is Guru Nanak. Mahala 2, Guru Angad. Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das.
Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das. Mahala 5, Guru Arjan, who compiled the book. And mahala 9, Guru Tegh Bahadur, whose hymns were added later.

There's no run of mahala 10 hymns: tradition says Guru Gobind Singh added his father's hymns, then gave the Guruship to the Granth itself, and his own writings are collected elsewhere. What does mahala mean?
Its meaning is debated. One common reading takes it from mahal, a house or dwelling: the first body, the fifth body. That fits the heart of it.
Sikhs understand the Gurus as one light, one jot, passing from one to the next, the way one lamp lights another.

The Granth itself says so, in the ballad of Satta and Balwand: the light is the same, the way is the same; only the body has changed. So when every Guru signs as Nanak, it isn't borrowing a well-known name.
It's saying the same light is speaking.

teach.h: THE BHAGATS SIGN THEIR OWN NAMES.
teach.b: The Bhagats, by contrast, sign with their own names: Kabir says, Ravidas says, Farid says.
The bottom line tells you it's the Nanak light speaking; the heading tells you through which Guru. Now you can read the map.

how: When a hymn is read in the gurdwara, the reader often announces its heading, such as Sorath mahala 5, so listeners know which Guru's words they are hearing; the hymn itself ends with the name Nanak.

games.q: a hymn ends: Nanak says. its heading reads Asa, mahala 5. who wrote it?
games.why: mahala 5 is Guru Arjan. he signs as Nanak because Sikhs understand the Gurus as one light, passed lamp to lamp.

practice: Picture a row of oil lamps in a dark room, one of them lit. Someone tips a second lamp toward it until the wick catches, then a third from the second, then a fourth, and the same flame moves down the row.
With each slow breath out, see one more lamp catch, until the room fills with light.

wordCard.voice: Mahala. The heading word with a number that tells you which Guru wrote a hymn, mahala 1 for Guru Nanak, mahala 5 for Guru Arjan, because every Guru signs as Nanak.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: mahala, the heading word followed by a number that tells which Guru wrote a hymn.

carryVoice: Your line: every guru signs as nanak. The number at the top names which one of them. That's day two hundred thirty-four.
